summary: A raptor on stilts: an eagle-headed bird that hunts on foot across African grasslands, striding up to 20–30 km a day and killing snakes and rodents with precise, lightning-fast kicks. It is the sole living member of its family.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, from Senegal and Sudan south to the Cape
abilities: Kills prey by stamping; a measured kick delivered about five times the bird's body weight in roughly 15 milliseconds
Hunts almost entirely on foot, walking long transects through grass to flush prey
Takes venomous snakes, protected by heavily scaled lower legs and very fast strikes
Flies strongly and soars, despite spending most of the day walking

animal.diet: Grasshoppers and other large insects, rodents, lizards, snakes, small birds and eggs
animal.habitat: Open grassland and lightly wooded savanna; avoids dense woodland
animal.lifespan: Around 10–15 years in the wild; longer in captivity
animal.size: About 1.2–1.5 m tall; wingspan about 2 m; 3–4 kg
animal.behaviour: Pairs patrol a territory side by side, stamping at tussocks to flush prey and then pinning it with repeated blows of the feet before swallowing it whole.
fieldMarks: Very long legs with black 'shorts' (feathered thighs) and bare pinkish lower legs
Pale grey body with black flight feathers
Bare orange-red facial skin around the eye
Loose crest of long black-tipped quills at the back of the head
Two very long central tail feathers projecting beyond the tail in flight
animal.voice: Usually silent; gives a deep, frog-like croak or groan, mainly in display or at the nest.
animal.lookalikes: At distance it may be taken for a crane or stork walking in grass, but neither has the hooked raptor bill, orange face, black thigh feathering or quill crest. In flight the long legs and elongated central tail feathers both trail beyond the tail, a combination no eagle shows.
animal.whereToSee: Open grasslands of Serengeti and Maasai Mara, Kruger's southern plains, Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park, Etosha and the Karoo
animal.season: Resident year-round; pairs nest on flat-topped acacias in most months

lore: The secretarybird appears on the coat of arms of South Africa adopted in 2000, its rising wings symbolising protection, and on the coat of arms of Sudan. Its English name is often linked to the quill-like crest resembling pens tucked behind a clerk's ear.
funFact: High-speed filming of a captive male showed each kick lasts about 15 milliseconds, shorter than a human blink, so the bird must aim before it strikes.

summary: One of Africa's most photographed birds: a stocky perch-hunter painted in turquoise, ultramarine, lilac and cinnamon, with two long tail streamers. It sits conspicuously on dead branches and drops onto insects and lizards on the ground.
nativeRange: Eastern and southern Africa, from Ethiopia and Somalia to northern South Africa and Namibia
abilities: Sit-and-wait hunter that spots small prey from exposed perches
Performs a tumbling, rolling display flight that gives rollers their name
Defends nest holes aggressively, diving at raptors and other intruders

animal.diet: Large insects, scorpions, centipedes, small lizards, frogs and occasionally small birds
animal.habitat: Acacia savanna and open woodland with scattered perches
animal.size: About 36 cm including tail streamers; 100–130 g
animal.behaviour: In display a bird climbs steeply and then dives with rocking, side-to-side rolls while calling harshly.
fieldMarks: Lilac throat and breast (blue-breasted in the northern subspecies lorti)
Turquoise belly, crown greenish, back cinnamon-brown
Brilliant ultramarine and turquoise wings, flashing in flight
Two long, thin, dark outer tail streamers
animal.voice: Harsh, grating 'rak' or 'kaak' calls, run together into a crackling series during the display flight.
animal.lookalikes: European roller (a winter visitor) has a blue head and breast and no tail streamers. Abyssinian roller has entirely blue underparts and even longer streamers and lives north of the equator. Racket-tailed roller has a blue breast and spatulate tips to its streamers. Purple roller is larger, with streaked purple-brown underparts and a square tail.
animal.whereToSee: Maasai Mara, Serengeti, Kruger, Okavango Delta, Chobe and Etosha; often on roadside dead trees

lore: Rollers take their common name from the tumbling display flight; the genus name Coracias comes from the Greek korakias, a kind of crow.
funFact: In the subspecies Coracias caudatus lorti of Ethiopia and Somalia the 'lilac' breast is blue, so not every lilac-breasted roller has one.

summary: A turkey-sized black hornbill with scarlet facial wattles that walks the savanna in family groups, hunting everything from beetles to tortoises and snakes. It is among the slowest-breeding birds in the world, with groups raising on average one chick every nine years.
nativeRange: Eastern and southern Africa, from Kenya and Burundi south to South Africa
abilities: Cooperative breeder: a dominant pair is helped by older offspring and other group members
Booming dawn chorus carries several kilometres across the savanna
Kills snakes, hares and tortoises with blows of its massive bill
Can live several decades, matching its very slow reproductive rate

animal.diet: Insects, reptiles including snakes and tortoises, frogs, small mammals and birds
animal.habitat: Savanna and grassland with large trees for nesting cavities
animal.lifespan: Several decades; captive birds have lived over 40 years
animal.behaviour: A group of 2–10 birds holds a large territory, walking together all day and booming in chorus at dawn to declare ownership.
fieldMarks: Very large all-black bird with white primaries visible in flight
Bright red bare skin on face and inflatable throat wattle
Females have a violet-blue patch on the throat
Heavy, down-curved black bill with low casque
Long eyelashes; walks on the ground like a turkey
animal.voice: A deep, resonant booming duet, 'oomph oomph-oomph', given mostly at dawn and audible several kilometres away.
animal.lookalikes: Abyssinian ground hornbill, north of the equator, has blue and red bare skin and an open-ended tubular casque. Distant birds are sometimes mistaken for turkeys or vultures on the ground, but the red face wattle is distinctive.
animal.whereToSee: Kruger National Park, Hluhluwe-iMfolozi, the Okavango and Serengeti; often walking in open grass
animal.season: Resident year-round; breeding in the southern summer rains

lore: Among Zulu and Xhosa peoples the bird is linked to rain and storms and is traditionally protected by taboo; its booming is said to forecast rain, and some communities would only kill one in times of drought.
funFact: Usually only one of the two eggs is raised; the second chick hatches days later and normally starves, which is why conservationists 'harvest' second chicks for captive rearing and reintroduction.

summary: A crane crowned with a halo of stiff golden feathers, famous for exuberant dancing. Uganda's national bird, it is one of only two cranes able to roost in trees.
nativeRange: Eastern and southern Africa, from Uganda and Kenya to South Africa
abilities: Long hind toe lets it grip branches and roost in trees, unlike most cranes
Elaborate dances of bowing, leaping and wing-flapping strengthen pair bonds
Inflates a red throat sac to produce a booming call

animal.diet: Omnivorous: seeds, grasses, insects, frogs, lizards and small fish
animal.habitat: Marshes, wet grassland and farmland near wetlands
animal.size: About 1 m tall; wingspan around 2 m; 3–4 kg
animal.behaviour: Pairs and flocks dance year-round, bobbing, bowing and leaping high into the air while tossing grass.
fieldMarks: Bare white cheek patch topped with red, and a small red throat wattle
White wings with golden and chestnut feathers
animal.voice: A honking, two-note 'mu-hem' or 'ya-oo' call; also a deep booming from the inflated throat sac.
animal.lookalikes: Black crowned crane (West and Central Africa, overlapping in Uganda and South Sudan) has a dark grey to black neck and body and a cheek patch that is white above and red below (red more extensive in the eastern subspecies), whereas the grey crowned crane's cheek is mostly white with only a small red patch at the top. Wattled crane is larger, lacks the golden crown and has long white feathered wattles.
animal.whereToSee: Uganda's wetlands (Mabamba, Lake Mburo), Ngorongoro Crater, Amboseli, KwaZulu-Natal Midlands
animal.season: Resident; breeds mainly in the rains

lore: The grey crowned crane is the national bird of Uganda and stands on the country's flag and coat of arms. Its Afrikaans name 'mahem' imitates the call.
funFact: Its population fell by more than half in about 45 years, largely through wetland drainage and capture for the live-bird trade.

summary: A white-headed sea eagle of African rivers and lakes whose ringing call is called 'the voice of Africa'. It snatches fish from the surface with a swing of its talons and is the national bird of Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia and South Sudan.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa wherever there is open fresh or coastal water
abilities: Grabs fish from just below the surface; spiny scales on its toes grip slippery prey
Can swim using its wings when a fish is too heavy to lift
Steals prey from herons, storks and other birds
Pairs duet with throws of the head, reinforcing territory along a stretch of shore

animal.diet: Mainly fish; also waterbirds, flamingos, carrion and young monitor lizards
animal.habitat: Large rivers, lakes, dams, swamps and coastal lagoons with tall perches
animal.size: 63–75 cm long; wingspan 2–2.4 m; females larger
animal.behaviour: It watches from a tree, then glides down and swings its feet forward at the last moment to pluck a fish within about 15 cm of the surface.
fieldMarks: Snow-white head, breast, back and short tail
Bare yellow face and yellow legs
Juveniles mottled brown and white, taking about five years to reach adult plumage
animal.voice: A loud, ringing, yelping 'weee-ah, hyo-hyo-hyo', given with the head thrown back over the shoulders, often as a pair duet.
animal.lookalikes: Palm-nut vulture is white with black wings but has a white belly, bare reddish face and a black-tipped tail. Madagascar fish eagle (Madagascar only) has a brown head and body. Immatures resemble other large brown eagles but usually show some white on the breast and tail.
animal.whereToSee: Lake Naivasha and Lake Baringo (Kenya), Chobe River, Okavango Delta, Lake Malawi, Lake Kariba, Murchison Falls

lore: The fish eagle appears on the coats of arms of Zambia, Namibia and South Sudan, and Zambia's flag shows it in flight; the Zulu name Inkwazi was given to the South African presidential aircraft.
funFact: Formerly placed in Haliaeetus with the bald eagle, it was moved by the IOC World Bird List in 2023 to Icthyophaga with the smaller tropical fish eagles, though not every checklist has followed.

summary: A glossy East African starling whose iridescent blue-green upperparts and orange belly are divided by a neat white band. Bold and sociable, it lives in cooperatively breeding groups and is a fixture of safari lodges.
nativeRange: East Africa: Ethiopia, Somalia, South Sudan, Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania
abilities: Cooperative breeder in which helpers, often relatives, feed the chicks
Iridescence is structural, produced by arrays of melanin granules in the feathers
Groups in unpredictable dry climates rely more on helpers, a link studied as a driver of cooperative breeding

animal.diet: Insects, especially termites and beetles, plus fruit and seeds
animal.habitat: Dry acacia savanna, thornbush, villages and lodge grounds
animal.behaviour: Groups forage on the ground in loose parties and build bulky domed nests of grass in thorny acacias.
fieldMarks: Narrow white band across the breast
animal.voice: A long, rambling warble of chattering and whistled phrases, often including mimicry; harsh 'chee-er' alarm.
animal.lookalikes: Hildebrandt's starling lacks the white breast band and has a red-orange eye. Shelley's starling has a darker chestnut belly, no white breast band and an orange eye. Golden-breasted starling has golden-yellow underparts and a long tail.
animal.whereToSee: Samburu, Tsavo, Amboseli and Maasai Mara (Kenya), Serengeti and Tarangire (Tanzania), Ethiopian Rift Valley

lore: It was described by Eduard Rüppell in 1845 from specimens collected in Ethiopia, and its tameness around camps and lodges has made it one of the most photographed birds in East Africa.
funFact: Long-term studies in Kenya found that superb starlings in good years and bad years shift between more and fewer helpers, a hedge against an unpredictable climate.

summary: A plain brown wading bird with a hammer-shaped head and the most extravagant nest of any bird its size: a domed stick mound more than a metre across. It is the only member of its family.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, Madagascar and south-western Arabia
abilities: Builds a domed nest of thousands of sticks, plastered with mud, with a side entrance and inner chamber
Pairs may build several such nests a year even when not breeding
Abandoned nests are taken over by owls, genets, snakes, bees and other animals

animal.diet: Mainly frogs and tadpoles, also small fish, shrimps and insects
animal.habitat: Shallow water edges of rivers, dams, pools and marshes with trees nearby
animal.behaviour: Groups perform 'false mounting' rituals, climbing on each other's backs, a behaviour not tied to mating.
fieldMarks: Backward-pointing crest balancing a heavy bill, giving a hammer-head profile
Fairly short black legs for a wader
Flies with neck slightly extended, often with a buoyant, soaring flight
animal.voice: A high, nasal 'yip' or 'kek' in flight; groups give excited, rising 'yip-purrr' chorus calls.
animal.lookalikes: Shape is unique. Distant birds may suggest a small heron or immature night heron, but no heron has the thick crest-and-bill hammer silhouette or uniform brown plumage.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any African wetland with trees: Kruger, Okavango Delta, Lake Naivasha, Murchison Falls; also western Madagascar

lore: In much of Africa the hamerkop is a bird of omen: a Zulu and Xhosa belief warns that harming it or its nest brings lightning or misfortune, and in Madagascar it is associated with bad luck.
funFact: A single hamerkop nest can take months to build, contain thousands of sticks, and is reputedly strong enough to bear the weight of a person.

summary: The smallest and by far the most numerous flamingo, gathering in pink rafts of hundreds of thousands on Africa's caustic soda lakes. It feeds almost entirely on microscopic cyanobacteria filtered from the surface water.
nativeRange: East and southern Africa's Rift Valley and salt pans; West Africa; north-western India and Pakistan
abilities: Filters cyanobacteria (chiefly Arthrospira, 'spirulina') with a deep-keeled bill held upside down
Breeds on the mudflats of hyperalkaline Lake Natron, where few predators can follow
Its pink colour comes from carotenoid pigments in its food
Flocks move hundreds of kilometres between lakes, mostly at night, following food

animal.diet: Cyanobacteria and benthic diatoms
animal.habitat: Alkaline and saline lakes, lagoons and salt pans
animal.behaviour: Huge flocks perform synchronised 'marching' displays, heads raised and turning in unison, before breeding.
fieldMarks: Deep pink plumage, often more strongly pink than the greater flamingo
Dark carmine-red bill that looks black at a distance
Deep red eye and facial skin
Crimson wing coverts and black flight feathers in flight
animal.voice: A high, goose-like murmuring 'murr-err' from feeding flocks; flight calls higher-pitched than greater flamingo.
animal.lookalikes: Greater flamingo is taller and paler, with a pale pink bill with a clean black tip, and a yellow eye. Lessers look compact with a uniformly dark bill.
animal.whereToSee: Lake Bogoria and Lake Nakuru (Kenya), Lake Natron (Tanzania), Etosha and Walvis Bay (Namibia), Kamfers Dam (South Africa), Little Rann of Kutch (India)
animal.season: Present year-round in the Rift Valley, moving between lakes; breeds at Lake Natron mainly from August to November

lore: The lesser flamingo's main breeding site at Lake Natron was threatened by a proposed soda-ash plant in the 2000s, which its developer dropped in 2008 after international campaigns, although the idea has resurfaced since.
funFact: Lake Natron's water can reach a pH above 10 and temperatures over 40 °C, yet it hosts the largest lesser flamingo breeding colonies on Earth.

summary: A drab woodland bird with an extraordinary partnership: it leads people to wild bees' nests and feeds on the wax left after the honey is taken. It is also a brood parasite whose chicks kill their foster siblings.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa outside the densest rainforest and driest deserts
abilities: Guides humans to bees' nests with a chattering call and short flights
Responds to specific human calls: Yao honey-hunters' 'brrr-hm' trill raises the chance of being guided
Can digest beeswax, a rare ability among vertebrates
Lays eggs in the nests of hole-nesting birds such as bee-eaters and barbets; the hatchling uses a hooked bill tip to kill host chicks

animal.diet: Beeswax, bee larvae and eggs, and insects
animal.habitat: Miombo and acacia woodland and savanna
animal.behaviour: When guiding, it flies ahead in short hops, calling and fanning its white-edged tail, and waits for its human followers to catch up.
fieldMarks: Male: pink bill, black throat and white ear patch
Grey-brown upperparts with a yellow shoulder patch in males
White outer tail feathers flashed in flight
Females and immatures plainer; juveniles have a yellow throat and breast
animal.voice: Male song a repeated, far-carrying 'vic-tor' or 'whit-purrr'; the guiding call is a persistent, dry chattering rattle.
animal.lookalikes: Lesser honeyguide is smaller, olive-tinged, with a stubby dark bill and no black throat. Scaly-throated honeyguide has a scaly-patterned throat. Juvenile greater honeyguides, with yellow throats, can be mistaken for other small yellow-throated birds.
animal.whereToSee: Niassa Special Reserve (Mozambique), where Yao honey-hunters still work with it; Hadza country around Lake Eyasi (Tanzania); miombo woodland in Zambia and Malawi

lore: Jesuit missionary João dos Santos described honeyguides eating candle wax in a Mozambique church in the 16th century. A 2016 study in Science showed that wild honeyguides learn and answer the Yao people's traditional honey-hunting call.
funFact: A 2023 study found that honeyguides in different regions have learned to respond to different local human calls, a cross-species culture.

summary: Africa's largest eagle, a powerful hunter of game birds, monitor lizards and small antelope. It hunts from a high soar, spotting prey from several kilometres away.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa, in open and semi-arid country
abilities: Exceptional eyesight; spots prey at a great distance while soaring
Kills prey as large as young antelope, jackals and monitor lizards
Uses enormous stick nests that may be reused for decades

animal.diet: Guineafowl, francolins, bustards, hyraxes, hares, monitor lizards, young antelope
animal.habitat: Savanna, thornbush and semi-desert with tall trees or pylons for nesting
animal.size: 78–96 cm long; wingspan about 1.9–2.6 m; 3–6 kg
animal.behaviour: It hunts mainly from a high, wide-circling soar, then drops in a long, shallow stoop on unsuspecting prey.
fieldMarks: Dark brown head, throat and upper breast forming a hood
White lower breast and belly lightly spotted with dark brown
Dark underwings in flight, contrasting with pale belly
animal.voice: Mostly silent; in display a loud, ringing 'klee-klee-klooee'.
animal.lookalikes: Black-chested snake eagle has a similar dark hood but an unspotted white belly, bare pale legs, a large round head with orange-yellow eyes and pale underwings. Juveniles are pale greyish-white below and can be confused with juvenile crowned eagles, which have barred legs and tails.
animal.whereToSee: Kruger and Kgalagadi (South Africa), Etosha (Namibia), Maasai Mara and Tsavo (Kenya)

lore: Its scientific name means 'warlike war-eagle'. Farmers have long persecuted it as a livestock killer; studies in Kruger tracked steep declines even inside protected areas.
funFact: Even in large reserves such as Kruger, martial eagle numbers fell by more than half in roughly two decades, prompting uplisting to Endangered in 2020.

summary: A carmine-and-turquoise bee-eater that nests in colonies of hundreds to thousands of burrows dug into riverbanks. It famously hunts insects flushed by grazing animals, sometimes riding on the backs of kori bustards.
nativeRange: Southern Africa from Angola and southern DR Congo to northern South Africa; spreads more widely after breeding
abilities: Excavates burrows usually 1–2 m long, sometimes more, into vertical sand cliffs
Rides on kori bustards, ostriches and large mammals to snatch flushed insects
Gathers at bush fires to catch fleeing insects
Removes the sting from bees and wasps by beating them on a perch

animal.diet: Flying insects: bees, wasps, locusts, grasshoppers, beetles, dragonflies
animal.habitat: River valleys, floodplains and savanna
animal.behaviour: Colonies of thousands of birds swirl above riverbanks, each pair digging its own tunnel side by side with neighbours.
animal.voice: Deep, throaty 'terk' or 'krik-krik' calls, given incessantly by flocks.
animal.lookalikes: Northern carmine bee-eater, north of the equator, has a blue-green throat rather than a carmine one. Other bee-eaters in its range are mostly green and none is carmine all over.
animal.whereToSee: Luangwa Valley (Zambia), Zambezi and Chobe rivers, Okavango Delta, Mana Pools (Zimbabwe)
animal.season: Intra-African migrant; breeds August to December in southern Africa, then disperses north and south

lore: Southern carmine bee-eater colonies on the Zambezi and Luangwa riverbanks are a celebrated attraction of the southern African dry season.
funFact: A breeding colony can number several thousand birds packed into a single sandbank.

summary: A fynbos endemic whose males trail tails nearly twice their body length. It is a key pollinator of proteas, pushing its long bill deep into the flowerheads for nectar.
nativeRange: Fynbos of the Western and Eastern Cape, South Africa
abilities: Pollinates many proteas and other fynbos plants while feeding on nectar
Males perform display flights with their tails flicked over their backs and wings rattling
Lines its nest with downy protea seed fluff

animal.diet: Nectar, especially of Protea, plus insects and spiders
animal.habitat: Mature fynbos with flowering proteas; gardens
animal.size: Males up to ~44 cm including tail; females ~29 cm
animal.behaviour: Males guard flowering protea patches from high perches and chase away rivals and sunbirds.
fieldMarks: Very long tail in males (shorter in females)
Brown upperparts with a brown-streaked white breast
White moustache and dark malar stripe
animal.voice: A jumble of harsh, grating and metallic notes; displaying males make a 'frrrt' wing rattle.
animal.lookalikes: Gurney's sugarbird, found further east in the eastern escarpment, has a rufous crown and breast and a shorter tail. Malachite sunbird males are green, not brown.
animal.whereToSee: Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden, Harold Porter Garden (Betty's Bay), Helderberg Nature Reserve, Cape Point
animal.season: Resident; breeds mainly in the winter rains (April–August)

lore: The sugarbirds form their own family found only in southern Africa, and the Cape sugarbird is an emblem of the Cape Floristic Region, one of the world's richest plant kingdoms.
funFact: Because fire periodically burns the fynbos and proteas take years to regrow and flower, sugarbirds move locally to follow mature, flowering protea stands.

summary: A grey, red-tailed parrot of West and Central African forests, renowned for its ability to mimic speech and to use words meaningfully. Capture for the pet trade has devastated wild populations.
nativeRange: Equatorial Africa from Côte d'Ivoire to western Kenya and Tanzania
abilities: Exceptional vocal mimic; captive birds learn hundreds of words
Shows abilities in categorisation, number and inference in laboratory studies
Gathers at dusk in communal roosts of hundreds to thousands
Visits forest clearings to eat clay, likely to aid digestion or mineral intake

animal.diet: Fruit, seeds and nuts, especially oil-palm fruits
animal.habitat: Lowland rainforest, forest edges, savanna woodland mosaics and mangroves
animal.behaviour: Flocks fly to communal roosts at dusk with loud screeches and whistles, often in pairs within the flock.
fieldMarks: Ash-grey body with paler scalloped head and neck
Bare white face patch around a pale yellow eye
animal.voice: Shrill whistles, screeches and clicks in flight; wild birds rarely mimic.
animal.lookalikes: Timneh parrot (West Africa, from Guinea to Côte d'Ivoire), now a separate species, is darker grey with a maroon tail and a horn-coloured upper mandible.
animal.whereToSee: Lobéké and Dja (Cameroon), Odzala-Kokoua (Republic of Congo), Kibale (Uganda), Príncipe island; forest clearings known as bais

lore: Irene Pepperberg's grey parrot Alex (1976–2007) could label objects, colours, shapes and quantities. The red tail feathers have long been used in Yoruba ritual and royal regalia.
funFact: Over a million wild-caught grey parrots are estimated to have entered international trade in recent decades; the species was moved to CITES Appendix I in 2016.

summary: A noisy, polka-dotted gamebird with a bony casque, living in flocks across African savanna. Domesticated in Africa and carried to Europe and the Americas, it is now kept and eaten worldwide.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa; introduced and domesticated widely
abilities: Eats ticks and insects, and is kept on farms partly for pest control
Flocks raise loud alarms that warn other animals of predators
Can run fast and roosts in trees at night

animal.diet: Seeds, bulbs, insects, ticks, snails
animal.habitat: Savanna, grassland, farmland and scrub
animal.behaviour: Flocks of dozens or even hundreds walk in long lines, calling raucously; they flee by running rather than flying.
fieldMarks: Slate-grey plumage covered in white spots
Bony, horn-coloured casque on top of the head
Bare blue and red head with wattles
animal.voice: A harsh, grating 'kek-kek-kek-krrrr' alarm and a rhythmic 'buck-wheat' call; flocks are very noisy.
animal.lookalikes: Crested guineafowl has a curly black crest instead of a casque. Vulturine guineafowl has a long, slim body, cobalt breast and a bare head with no casque.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any savanna reserve in East and southern Africa; Kruger, Serengeti, Etosha

lore: Greek myth said the sisters of the hero Meleager wept for him and were turned into guineafowl, their tears becoming the white spots, hence 'meleagris'. Romans knew it as the Numidian hen.
funFact: The turkey's genus name Meleagris was borrowed from the classical name of the guineafowl, a legacy of early European confusion between the two birds.

summary: The largest guineafowl, with a vulture-like bare head and long cobalt-and-white hackle feathers. Researchers found that it lives in a multilevel society, a social structure once thought limited to large-brained mammals.
nativeRange: Dry north-eastern Africa: Ethiopia, Somalia, Kenya and north-eastern Tanzania
abilities: Forms stable groups that associate in a structured multilevel society
Can survive with little drinking water, getting moisture from its food
Group decisions about direction are influenced by many members rather than only dominants

animal.diet: Seeds, fruit, leaves and invertebrates
animal.habitat: Dry bush and grassland, often along riverine woodland
animal.behaviour: Groups of 15–60 birds roost together in trees and merge into larger supergroups at certain times.
fieldMarks: Bare blue-grey head with a chestnut nape patch
Long cobalt-blue, white and black striped hackles over the neck and back
animal.voice: Harsh, chinking 'chink-chink-chink' alarms and loud scolding chatter.
animal.lookalikes: Helmeted guineafowl is dumpier, with a bony casque and evenly spotted grey plumage, and lacks the striped hackles and blue breast.
animal.whereToSee: Samburu, Buffalo Springs and Shaba (Kenya), Tsavo East, Meru, Awash (Ethiopia)

lore: Research at Mpala Research Centre in Kenya, published in 2019, described the first known multilevel society in a bird, comparing vulturine guineafowl to primates and elephants.
funFact: Its 'vulture' head lacks feathers, a probable adaptation for losing heat in hot dry country.

summary: A sparrow-sized bird that builds the largest nests of any bird: colossal communal haystacks in camelthorn trees, housing hundreds of birds in separate chambers. The nest buffers temperatures in the Kalahari's searing days and freezing nights.
nativeRange: Southern Africa: Namibia, Botswana and South Africa (Kalahari and Karoo)
abilities: Builds nests weighing up to around a tonne, with up to 100 or more separate chambers
Nest interiors stay much warmer at night and cooler by day than outside
Colonies may be used for many decades, some for over a century
Provides homes for pygmy falcons, lovebirds, finches and reptiles

animal.diet: Insects, especially termites, plus seeds
animal.habitat: Arid savanna with large trees such as camelthorn (Vachellia erioloba), also telephone poles
animal.behaviour: Members of a colony continually add straw to the roof and maintain individual chambers; helpers feed young.
fieldMarks: Scalloped back pattern with dark feathers edged pale
animal.voice: Chattering, twittering contact calls around the colony; a 'chip-chip' in flight.
animal.lookalikes: Scaly-feathered weaver (scaly-feathered finch) is smaller with a white moustache and black stripes, and lacks the black throat. House sparrows lack the scaly flanks and black chin.
animal.whereToSee: Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park, Augrabies Falls, Kalahari roads in Namibia (nests on telephone poles), Etosha

lore: The French naturalist François Le Vaillant described the giant nests in the 1780s; the bird's French name, républicain, likens a colony to a republic.
funFact: Large nests can collapse the trees that hold them, especially after rain soaks the straw.

summary: Probably the most abundant wild bird on Earth, with a post-breeding population estimated at around 1.5 billion. Its vast flocks, darkening the sky, can strip a grain field in hours, earning it the name 'feathered locust'.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa outside rainforest and true desert
abilities: Forms flocks of millions that move with seasonal rains to follow ripening grass seed
Breeding colonies can contain millions of nests across many hectares
Chicks can leave the nest about two weeks after hatching

animal.diet: Grass seeds, cultivated grains and insects
animal.habitat: Dry savanna, grassland and cultivated land
animal.behaviour: Feeding flocks 'roll' across the ground as birds at the back leapfrog over those in front.
fieldMarks: Thick, conical red bill (yellowish in breeding females)
Breeding males: black (or pale) face mask framed by pink or buff
animal.voice: Constant chattering twitter from flocks; male song a jumbled, harsh warble.
animal.lookalikes: Red-headed and cardinal queleas are smaller-billed, with red heads in breeding males. Non-breeding bishops and widowbirds look similar but have dark or horn-coloured bills, not red.
animal.whereToSee: Large flocks across Kalahari, Etosha, Serengeti, the Sahel, especially near water in the dry season
animal.season: Present year-round, moving nomadically with rains; breeds in the wet season

lore: Quelea control, using aerial spraying and explosives at roosts, has been a major agricultural programme across Africa since the mid-20th century.
funFact: Despite control operations killing many millions of birds each year, the quelea's overall population has not noticeably declined.

summary: A large griffon vulture of the Sahel and East Africa and the highest-flying bird on record. Specialist haemoglobin lets it breathe at altitudes where a human would lose consciousness.
nativeRange: Sahel and East Africa, from Senegal to Ethiopia and Tanzania
abilities: Struck an airliner at 11,300 m over Côte d'Ivoire in 1973, the highest-flying bird recorded
Has a haemoglobin variant that binds oxygen well at low pressure
Clears carcasses fast, limiting the spread of disease
Soars on thermals for hours while searching for food

animal.diet: Carrion, especially soft tissue of large mammals
animal.habitat: Open savanna and grassland, nesting on cliffs
animal.behaviour: Colonies breed on high cliffs and forage over vast areas, often travelling 150 km from the nest.
fieldMarks: Dark brown body with every feather edged creamy-white, giving a scaly, mottled look
In flight, thin white lines across the underwing
animal.voice: Hissing, squealing and grunting at carcasses; otherwise silent.
animal.lookalikes: White-backed vulture has plainer, less scaled brown plumage, a dark bill and dark eye, and a white rump in flight. Lappet-faced vulture is larger with a bare pink head and wrinkled lappets.
animal.whereToSee: Serengeti, Maasai Mara, Simien Mountains (Ethiopia), Gol Mountains (Tanzania) for cliff colonies
animal.season: Resident; moves to follow migratory herds

lore: It is named after the German explorer Eduard Rüppell, who collected in north-east Africa in the 1820s. Vulture parts are used in African traditional medicine and divination, which drives poaching.
funFact: Its population dropped by an estimated 97% in three generations, mostly through poisoning, including poachers lacing elephant carcasses so circling vultures won't reveal them.

summary: One of the world's rarest birds of prey, confined to a few lakes, rivers and mangroves of western Madagascar. Pairs are sometimes helped at the nest by additional adults.
nativeRange: Western Madagascar
abilities: Hunts fish from tall waterside perches
Some pairs breed with help from extra adult birds

animal.diet: Mainly fish, especially native species and introduced tilapia
animal.habitat: Large lakes, rivers, estuaries and mangroves with tall trees
animal.behaviour: Pairs defend a lake shore and call loudly from high perches.
fieldMarks: Brown body with pale brownish-white cheeks and throat
animal.voice: A loud, high, yelping call, similar to the African fish eagle's but harsher and more rapid.
animal.lookalikes: No similar large eagle occurs in its range. Madagascar harrier-hawk is smaller, grey and long-legged.
animal.whereToSee: Tsimembo-Manambolomaty lakes complex (western Madagascar), Antsalova region

lore: The Peregrine Fund and local communities have run Madagascar fish eagle projects since the 1990s, combining surveys with community-managed lake protections.
funFact: It is the closest relative of the African fish eagle, from which its ancestors likely arrived on Madagascar.

summary: A rainforest bird of north-eastern Madagascar carrying a huge, arched, bright blue bill. Vangas are a spectacular radiation of birds found only on Madagascar.
nativeRange: Lowland and mid-altitude rainforest of north-eastern Madagascar
abilities: Uses its massive bill to seize large insects, lizards and frogs
Part of the vanga radiation, whose bill shapes span the range of many bird families

animal.diet: Large insects, chameleons, geckos and frogs
animal.habitat: Undisturbed lowland and mid-elevation rainforest
animal.behaviour: Sits still in the mid-canopy for long periods before sallying for prey.
animal.voice: A long, accelerating, whistled trill descending toward the end.
animal.lookalikes: No other bird has this bill. Rufous vanga is smaller, with a white breast and pale blue-grey bill.
animal.whereToSee: Masoala National Park and Marojejy National Park

lore: It was named in honour of the French artist Florent Prévost; it remains a prized bird for birders visiting Masoala.
funFact: It is the only member of the genus Euryceros, one of the vangas, a family that radiated into many bill shapes on Madagascar.

summary: The only penguin that breeds in Africa, nesting on islands and beaches from Namibia to Algoa Bay. In 2024 it became the first penguin species classified as Critically Endangered.
nativeRange: Coasts and islands of Namibia and South Africa
abilities: Dives to around 130 m and swims at up to about 20 km/h
Has bare pink skin above the eye that helps shed heat
Nests in burrows dug into guano or under bushes

animal.diet: Sardines, anchovies and other small shoaling fish
animal.habitat: Rocky islands, sheltered beaches and the Benguela current
animal.behaviour: Pairs reunite at the same burrow each season and greet each other with loud braying.
fieldMarks: Single black band across the chest
Bare pink skin patch above the eye
White stripe curving from above the eye to the breast
Unique black spots on the chest
animal.voice: A loud, donkey-like braying, given with the head thrown back.
animal.lookalikes: Magellanic penguin (South America) has two chest bands; Humboldt penguin has a broader pink face and one band. No other penguin breeds in Africa.
animal.whereToSee: Boulders Beach (Simon's Town), Stony Point (Betty's Bay), Robben Island, Bird Island in Algoa Bay
animal.season: Present year-round; breeds in most months, with peaks varying by colony

lore: Its nests were destroyed by 19th- and 20th-century guano harvesting and its eggs collected for food; millions of eggs were taken from Dassen Island alone.
funFact: The breeding population has fallen below 10,000 pairs, down from perhaps over a million birds a century ago.

summary: A striking eagle with almost no tail, red face and legs, and a rocking, tightrope-walker flight. It spends much of the day gliding low over the savanna searching for carrion and prey.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa and south-western Arabia
abilities: Glides for hours, tilting from side to side, with little flapping
Spreads its wings in 'heraldic' sunbathing postures
Finds carcasses and is often first at them

animal.diet: Carrion, birds, small mammals, reptiles
animal.habitat: Open savanna and woodland
animal.behaviour: It flies with wings held in a shallow V, rocking side to side, a habit that inspired its French name meaning 'acrobat'.
fieldMarks: Very short tail; feet project past it in flight
Black body with chestnut back (cream in some birds)
Females have grey secondaries, males black
animal.voice: A loud, barking 'kaw-aw' and a harsh 'schaaaw'.
animal.lookalikes: Black-chested snake eagle has a long tail and white belly. Juvenile bateleurs are brown and may resemble other brown eagles but share the short-tailed silhouette.
animal.whereToSee: Kruger, Kgalagadi, Okavango, Serengeti, Maasai Mara

lore: François Le Vaillant named it 'bateleur' (French for a street acrobat) in the 18th century because of its tilting flight.
funFact: Bateleurs can spend 8–9 hours a day in the air and cover hundreds of kilometres.

summary: A massive, bald-headed stork that scavenges carcasses and rubbish dumps alongside vultures. Its wingspan rivals the largest of any land bird.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa
abilities: Wingspan regularly exceeds 2.5 m and is reported up to 3 m or more
Inflates an air-filled neck sac in display
Has adapted to towns, scavenging dumps and fish markets
Takes live prey including flamingos, frogs and rodents

animal.diet: Carrion, refuse, fish, frogs, rodents and birds
animal.habitat: Savanna, wetlands, fishing villages and cities
animal.behaviour: In cities like Kampala, marabous nest in trees along streets and patrol rubbish dumps.
fieldMarks: Bald, pinkish head and neck, often with scabby spots
Dark grey back and wings, white underparts
Long grey legs often whitened with excreta
animal.voice: Mostly silent; clatters its bill and gives croaks and grunts.
animal.lookalikes: Saddle-billed stork is colourful with a red-and-black bill. Vultures share the bald head but have hooked bills and short legs.
animal.whereToSee: Kampala (Uganda), Lake Naivasha, Serengeti, Maasai Mara, Kruger, Chobe

lore: Fluffy marabou undertail feathers were widely traded in the 19th and 20th centuries for hats and trimmings; 'marabou' became a name for any fluffy trim.
funFact: Marabous cool their legs by excreting on them, a habit known as urohidrosis.

summary: The world's largest kingfisher, famous for its raucous family chorus of 'laughter' at dawn and dusk. It rarely fishes, instead dropping onto snakes, lizards and insects from a perch.
nativeRange: Eastern Australia; introduced to south-western Western Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand
abilities: Kills snakes and lizards by bashing them against branches or dropping them
Family groups 'laugh' together to proclaim territory
Cooperative breeder: older offspring help raise new chicks

animal.diet: Insects, worms, lizards, snakes, small mammals and birds
animal.habitat: Dry eucalypt woodland, open forest, parks and gardens
animal.behaviour: Groups of related birds call in chorus, one starting with low chuckles before the rest join in a crescendo of laughter.
fieldMarks: Large, stocky kingfisher with a massive bill
Off-white head with a dark brown eye-stripe
Brown wings with a small pale-blue shoulder patch
animal.voice: A loud, rollicking 'koo-koo-koo-ka-ka-ka' that rises into raucous laughter, often by several birds at once, especially at dawn and dusk.
animal.lookalikes: Blue-winged kookaburra (northern Australia) has a pale eye, no dark eye-stripe, a blue rump and more extensive blue in the wing, and a harsher, cackling call.
animal.whereToSee: Common in eastern Australian bushland, parks and gardens from Queensland to Victoria; Royal National Park (Sydney), Lamington National Park

lore: The name comes from the Wiradjuri word guuguubarra, imitating its call. A widely retold Aboriginal story says the kookaburra's laughter is the signal for the sky-people to light the sun each morning.
funFact: Its call has been widely used as a 'jungle' sound effect in films, even those set nowhere near Australia.

summary: A towering, flightless rainforest bird with a bony casque and a dagger-like inner claw. It is a crucial seed disperser for rainforest trees, swallowing fruit whole and depositing seeds far away.
nativeRange: Northern Queensland, New Guinea and nearby islands
abilities: Disperses seeds of more than 200 plant species, some almost entirely dependent on it
Inner toe bears a claw up to about 12 cm long, a formidable weapon
Low-frequency booming calls may be partly below human hearing
Swims well and can run at up to around 50 km/h through forest

animal.diet: Fallen fruit, fungi, invertebrates and small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Tropical rainforest, swamp forest, adjacent woodland
animal.lifespan: Up to about 40 years in captivity
animal.size: 1.5–1.8 m tall; females up to about 60–70 kg
animal.behaviour: The male alone incubates the eggs for about 50 days and raises the striped chicks for up to nine months.
fieldMarks: Bright blue neck with two red wattles
Massive grey legs with three toes
animal.voice: Deep, rumbling booms and low hisses; mostly heard at close range.
animal.lookalikes: Emu is grey-brown and lacks the casque and wattles; it lives in open country. In New Guinea, northern and dwarf cassowaries have different wattle patterns (one or none).
animal.whereToSee: Mission Beach and Etty Bay (Queensland), Daintree, Cape York; New Guinea lowlands

lore: A 2021 study of ancient eggshell suggested people in New Guinea may have collected and raised cassowary chicks as long as 18,000 years ago, and cassowary-bone daggers were made there into the 20th century.
funFact: Although listed as Least Concern globally, the Australian population is listed as Endangered under Australian law.

summary: Australia's tallest bird and the world's second-tallest, a shaggy-feathered nomad of the outback. It walks long distances following rain, and the male raises the chicks alone.
nativeRange: Mainland Australia
abilities: Can run at about 50 km/h
Makes long nomadic movements following rains
Males incubate eggs for around eight weeks, barely eating or drinking
Females make deep drumming calls via an inflatable throat sac

animal.diet: Fruit, seeds, flowers, green shoots and insects
animal.habitat: Most habitats except dense rainforest and the driest deserts
animal.behaviour: After laying, the female leaves and may mate again, while the male guards the clutch and then the striped chicks for months.
fieldMarks: Tiny vestigial wings, hidden in the plumage
animal.voice: Females make a deep, booming drum or thump; males grunt.
animal.lookalikes: Southern cassowary (rainforest, Queensland) is black with a casque and blue-and-red neck. Ostriches (feral, rare) have black-and-white or brown plumage and two-toed feet.
animal.whereToSee: Common in outback NSW, Queensland and Western Australia; Wilsons Promontory, Tower Hill (Victoria), Kalbarri

lore: Many Aboriginal peoples see the 'Emu in the Sky', formed by dark dust lanes of the Milky Way. In 1932 Western Australian authorities waged the so-called 'Emu War' with machine guns and largely failed.
funFact: The emu appears on Australia's coat of arms alongside the red kangaroo.

summary: A pink-and-grey cockatoo of inland Australia, abundant and gregarious. It has spread with farming and watering points to occupy nearly the entire continent.
nativeRange: Across mainland Australia; introduced to Tasmania
abilities: Expanded its range greatly with land clearing, crops and artificial water
Forms long-lasting pair bonds
Highly social, roosting in large flocks and performing acrobatics on wires

animal.diet: Seeds, grain, roots and shoots
animal.habitat: Open country, farmland, parks and towns
animal.behaviour: Flocks hang upside down, swing on wires and roll in the rain, behaviour widely described as play.
fieldMarks: Deep rose-pink face, neck and underparts
Pale pink crown with a short crest
animal.voice: Shrill, high-pitched 'chet' or 'chee' screeches.
animal.lookalikes: Major Mitchell's (pink) cockatoo is white and salmon-pink, with a tall red-and-yellow banded crest.
animal.whereToSee: Almost anywhere in Australia; country towns, sports fields and farmland

lore: The name 'galah' comes from the Yuwaalaraay word gilaa. In Australian slang, 'galah' means a fool or loudmouth.
funFact: Galahs often pair for life, and both partners share incubation and chick-rearing.

summary: A noisy, rainbow-coloured parrot with a brush-tipped tongue for lapping nectar and pollen. Common in eastern Australian cities, it is an important pollinator of eucalypts and banksias.
nativeRange: Eastern and south-eastern Australia; introduced to Perth and New Zealand
abilities: Brush-tipped tongue collects nectar and pollen
Pollinates many eucalypts, banksias and grevilleas
Forms huge, noisy communal roosts in city trees

animal.diet: Nectar, pollen, fruit, flowers and some insects
animal.habitat: Woodland, forest edges, parks and gardens
animal.behaviour: Flocks swirl through the canopy screeching, following flowering trees.
animal.voice: Shrill, screeching 'chee-chee' and constant chatter.
animal.lookalikes: Red-collared lorikeet (northern Australia) has an orange collar and black belly. Scaly-breasted lorikeet is green with yellow scalloping.
animal.whereToSee: Common in Sydney, Brisbane, Gold Coast; Currumbin Wildlife Sanctuary

lore: At Currumbin on the Gold Coast, public lorikeet feeding has drawn visitors since the 1940s. In Perth, escaped birds became an invasive pest.
funFact: Rainbow lorikeets have been recorded catching and eating meat, which may be linked to diet shortages.

summary: A black-and-white songbird whose rich, carolling song is one of the iconic sounds of Australia. It is notorious for swooping people during nesting season.
nativeRange: Australia and southern New Guinea; introduced to New Zealand
abilities: Complex warbling and carolling song with mimicry
Remembers individual human faces
Groups defend territories year-round
Shows strong cooperation, including helping to remove tracking devices from one another

animal.diet: Insects, grubs, worms and small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Open country with scattered trees, parks and farms
animal.behaviour: During nesting, some males swoop pedestrians and cyclists who come near.
fieldMarks: White or grey nape and back (varies regionally)
Pale bluish-grey bill with dark tip
animal.voice: A rich, flute-like carolling, often by groups; also complex warbles and mimicry.
animal.lookalikes: Pied currawong is mostly black with a yellow eye and white tail tip. Magpie-lark is smaller, with a thin bill and white eyebrow or throat.
animal.whereToSee: Common in parks and playing fields throughout Australia

lore: Noongar stories tell of Koolbardi the magpie and Wardong the crow. The magpie is the emblem of many Australian sports teams.
funFact: In 2022 researchers reported that magpies removed tracking harnesses from one another, an unusual example of cooperative rescue.

summary: A tiny, cocked-tailed bird whose breeding males glow electric blue. Its family life is famous for cooperative breeding and very high rates of extra-pair mating.
nativeRange: South-eastern Australia and Tasmania
abilities: Cooperative breeding, with helpers raising the young
Mothers teach embryos a 'password' call in the egg
Males pluck yellow petals and display them to females

animal.diet: Insects and other small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Dense shrubs and grassland edges, gardens
animal.behaviour: Mothers call to eggs before hatching, and chicks incorporate a unique 'password' into their begging calls.
fieldMarks: Breeding males: bright blue crown, cheeks and mantle
Females and non-breeding males brown with orange-red around the eye
animal.voice: A high, rapid, reeling trill.
animal.lookalikes: Splendid fairywren males are blue all over. Variegated fairywren has chestnut shoulders. Females of other fairywrens differ in eye patches and tail colour.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and parks in Melbourne, Canberra, Sydney, Hobart; Royal Botanic Gardens

lore: Known to generations of Australians as the 'blue wren', it is a fixture of suburban gardens; a 2012 study showing that mothers teach their embryos a 'password' call drew worldwide attention.
funFact: Despite living in pairs, most chicks in a superb fairywren nest are fathered by males outside the pair.

summary: A New Zealand honeyeater with iridescent plumage and a white throat tuft. Its complex song, with clicks, chimes and wheezes, comes from two voice boxes.
nativeRange: New Zealand
abilities: Two-sided syrinx lets it sing two notes at once
Some song elements are reported to be too high-pitched for people to hear
Pollinates flax, kōwhai and other native plants
Accomplished mimic, including human speech

animal.diet: Nectar, fruit, insects
animal.habitat: Native forest, regenerating scrub, parks and gardens
animal.behaviour: Tūī are aggressive defenders of nectar trees, chasing off other birds with loud wing whirring.
fieldMarks: Dark iridescent plumage with blue, green and bronze sheen
Lacy white collar of filamentous feathers
animal.voice: A rich mix of bell-like notes, clicks, cackles and wheezes.
animal.lookalikes: Korimako (New Zealand bellbird) is smaller, olive-green and lacks the white tufts.
animal.whereToSee: Zealandia (Wellington), Tiritiri Matangi, Otari-Wilton's Bush, Auckland parks

lore: Māori trained captive tūī to recite karakia and greetings. 'Parson bird' refers to the white tufts resembling clerical bands.
funFact: Like other songbirds, the tūī has a two-sided voice box (syrinx), but it uses it with unusual virtuosity, producing two independent sounds at once.

summary: The world's only alpine parrot, an olive-green clown of New Zealand's Southern Alps. Famously curious and clever, kea solve puzzles, use tools and even have a 'play' call that sets other kea romping.
nativeRange: South Island, New Zealand
abilities: Solves multi-step puzzles and uses tools in experiments
Its 'warble' call triggers play in other kea, an emotional contagion
Understands statistical probabilities in choice tasks
Survives in cold, snowy mountain habitats

animal.diet: Roots, leaves, fruit, insects, carrion
animal.habitat: Alpine and subalpine forest, scrub, grassland
animal.behaviour: Young kea gather in groups to explore and play, tearing car parts and backpacks.
animal.voice: A loud, descending 'kee-aaa' call, from which its name derives.
animal.lookalikes: Kākā is reddish-brown, lives in lowland forest, and has a heavier bill.
animal.whereToSee: Arthur's Pass, Homer Tunnel (Milford Road), Aoraki/Mount Cook

lore: Farmers accused kea of killing sheep, and a bounty killed some 150,000 birds between 1860 and 1970.
funFact: Kea are one of the few non-primate animals shown to make statistical inferences.

summary: A large, flightless rail with brilliant blue-green plumage and a heavy red bill. Thought extinct for half a century, it was rediscovered in 1948 in New Zealand's Murchison Mountains.
nativeRange: South Island, New Zealand
abilities: Flightless and long-lived
Feeds on tussock grasses, snipping off tender bases
Recovered from near extinction through intensive conservation

animal.diet: Tussock grasses, herbs, rhizomes
animal.habitat: Alpine grassland, now also predator-free islands and sanctuaries
animal.behaviour: Pairs defend territories and raise one to two chicks each year.
fieldMarks: Massive red bill and frontal shield
animal.voice: Loud, resonant hooting and clucking contact calls, often exchanged between pair members; deeper than the pūkeko's screech.
animal.lookalikes: Pūkeko is slimmer, with long legs and a smaller bill, and can fly.
animal.whereToSee: Tiritiri Matangi Island, Zealandia, Orokonui Ecosanctuary, Burwood Takahē Centre

lore: Geoffrey Orbell rediscovered the takahē in 1948 near Lake Te Anau, 50 years after it was believed extinct.
funFact: The total population passed 500 birds in 2023 and was estimated at about 529 at the end of 2024, thanks to translocations and predator control.

summary: Australia's largest bird of prey, with a distinctive diamond-shaped tail. It soars on thermals for hours and is revered in Aboriginal cultures.
nativeRange: Australia, southern New Guinea
abilities: Soars on thermals to great heights
Hunts cooperatively to take prey like kangaroos and goats
Builds huge stick nests up to 2 m across

animal.diet: Rabbits, wallabies, kangaroos, birds, reptiles, carrion
animal.habitat: Woodland, savanna and open country
animal.behaviour: Pairs soar together, performing undulating flights and talon-grappling displays.
fieldMarks: Very large, dark brown to black plumage
animal.voice: Mostly silent; gives whistling yelps.
animal.lookalikes: Little eagle is much smaller with a square-cut tail and pale underwing band. Black kite has a shallow forked tail and slender build. Black-breasted buzzard has white 'bullseye' windows in the primaries and a short square tail. Only the wedge-tail shows the long diamond-shaped tail.
animal.whereToSee: Outback Australia; Flinders Ranges, Kakadu, Tasmania

lore: To the Kulin nations of Victoria, Bunjil the wedge-tailed eagle is the creator ancestor. The Tasmanian subspecies is listed as Endangered.
funFact: Wedge-tailed eagles have been known to attack hang-gliders and drones.

summary: A nocturnal bird often mistaken for an owl, famous for its broken-branch camouflage. It has a wide, frog-like bill and hunts insects at night.
nativeRange: Throughout Australia and Tasmania
abilities: Mimics a broken branch when threatened
Night hunter catching insects with its wide bill
Mated pairs roost together for years

animal.diet: Insects, worms, spiders, small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Woodland, forest, parks and gardens
animal.behaviour: By day it perches motionless, closing its eyes to slits and stretching its body to blend with branches.
animal.voice: A low, repetitive 'oom-oom-oom'.
animal.lookalikes: Owls have hooked bills and strong talons; papuan frogmouth is larger with red eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Parks and gardens across Australia

lore: Early settlers often called it 'mopoke', a name that belongs to the southern boobook owl; the boobook's 'mo-poke' call was long wrongly attributed to the frogmouth.
funFact: Despite its look, the tawny frogmouth is more closely related to nightjars than to owls.

summary: A black-and-white bird famed as one of Australia's finest songsters. It impales prey on thorns and sings complex duets.
nativeRange: Mainland Australia (except far south-east)
abilities: Sings complex fluty duets and choruses
Impales prey on thorns or wedges it in branches
Mimics other birds

animal.diet: Insects, small reptiles, birds, mice
animal.habitat: Open woodland and farmland
animal.behaviour: It stores food by wedging prey in tree forks or impaling it on thorns.
animal.voice: Rich, flute-like piping, often in duets.
animal.lookalikes: Grey butcherbird lacks the black bib. Australian magpie is larger and lacks the hook-tipped bill.
animal.whereToSee: Inland Queensland, NSW, Northern Territory

lore: Violinist and zoomusicologist Hollis Taylor spent years transcribing its songs in the outback for her 2017 book 'Is Birdsong Music?'.
funFact: Pied butcherbird songs vary from region to region and change from year to year, with individual birds reworking phrases like improvising musicians.

summary: A striking black-and-gold honeyeater of south-eastern Australia's box-ironbark woodlands, now so rare that many males never hear an adult of their own species and fail to learn its song. Fewer than about 300 are thought to remain in the wild.
nativeRange: South-eastern Australia, mainly inland slopes of the Great Dividing Range in New South Wales and Victoria
abilities: Pollinates flowering eucalypts such as mugga ironbark, yellow box and white box while feeding on nectar
Tracks irregular eucalypt flowering across hundreds of kilometres
Young males learn song from adults, which is why the song is fading as numbers fall

animal.diet: Nectar, especially of eucalypts and mistletoe; also lerp, honeydew and insects
animal.habitat: Dry box-ironbark eucalypt woodland and riparian forest
animal.behaviour: In a 2021 study, around 12% of wild males sang the songs of other species, such as friarbirds and wattlebirds, rather than their own, having had no regent honeyeater tutors.
fieldMarks: Black head, neck and upper breast
Pale yellow scalloping on back and breast
Bright yellow edges to wing and tail feathers
Bare, warty pinkish skin around the eye
animal.voice: A soft, bell-like, metallic warble; males that have not learned it may give mimicked songs of other honeyeaters instead.
animal.lookalikes: Painted honeyeater has a pink bill, plain black upperparts and unscalloped white underparts. New Holland honeyeater has white-streaked underparts, a white eye and yellow wing panels but no bare facial skin.
animal.whereToSee: Capertee Valley and Hunter Valley (NSW), Chiltern-Mt Pilot National Park (Victoria); release sites in north-east Victoria
animal.season: Nomadic resident; movements follow eucalypt flowering

lore: Taronga Zoo has bred regent honeyeaters for release since the 1990s, and captive young are now tutored with recordings of wild song before release.
funFact: It is one of the first wild birds documented losing its song culture because the population became too small and scattered for young males to find tutors.

summary: A big, iridescent green-and-white pigeon whose wingbeats whoosh through New Zealand forests. With other large fruit-eating birds extinct, it is the only native bird able to swallow the largest forest fruits whole, making it vital for spreading the seeds of trees such as taraire and tawa.
nativeRange: New Zealand
abilities: Swallows fruits up to about 2.5 cm across and disperses their seeds
Main or sole disperser of large-fruited native trees including taraire, tawa, karaka and miro
Performs steep, swooping display flights, stalling at the top before diving

animal.diet: Fruit, leaves, buds and flowers of native and introduced plants
animal.habitat: Native forest, scrub, farmland with trees, parks and gardens
animal.behaviour: After gorging on fermenting fruit in summer, kererū are sometimes found too intoxicated to fly properly.
fieldMarks: Large pigeon with iridescent green-bronze head, throat and upperparts
Clean white breast and belly, sharply divided from the green bib
animal.voice: Mostly silent; a soft, low 'ooo' coo. The noisy swish of the wings is usually heard first.
animal.lookalikes: Feral rock pigeons are smaller and grey. On the Chatham Islands the related parea is about a fifth larger, paler on the back, with a pale grey rump and an orange-tipped bill.
animal.whereToSee: Zealandia and Otari-Wilton's Bush (Wellington), Tiritiri Matangi, Christchurch Botanic Gardens, native forest throughout New Zealand

lore: Kererū were an important traditional food for Māori, harvested under seasonal restrictions, and their feathers were woven into cloaks; the bird is now fully protected. It was voted New Zealand's Bird of the Year in 2018.
funFact: Because no surviving native bird can swallow fruit as large, the decline of kererū could leave several of New Zealand's biggest-fruited trees with no natural seed disperser.

summary: A sooty-black swan with a scarlet bill and white flight feathers, native to Australia. To Europeans it was proverbial for an impossible thing until Dutch sailors saw it on Western Australia's Swan River in 1697.
nativeRange: Southern and eastern Australia and Tasmania; introduced to New Zealand
abilities: Nomadic: moves long distances, often at night, to reach newly filled wetlands
Can breed at almost any time of year when water conditions suit
Moults all its flight feathers at once and is briefly flightless

animal.diet: Aquatic plants, algae and pasture grasses
animal.habitat: Lakes, swamps, estuaries and coastal lagoons, fresh to brackish
animal.lifespan: Commonly over 20 years in the wild; up to about 40 in captivity
animal.behaviour: Pairs build huge floating or reed-island nests and share incubation; the downy grey cygnets often ride on a parent's back.
fieldMarks: All-black body with curled, ruffled wing feathers on the back
Bright red bill with a white band near the tip
White primary and secondary flight feathers, flashing in flight
Very long neck held in an S-curve
animal.voice: A high, musical, bugling 'whoo-ah' given on the water and in flight; hisses when threatened.
animal.lookalikes: Mute swan (introduced in Western Australia and elsewhere) is white with an orange bill. No other black-bodied bird of its size has a red bill and long neck.
animal.whereToSee: Swan River and Herdsman Lake (Perth), Coorong (South Australia), Lake Ellesmere / Te Waihora (New Zealand), Albert Park Lake (Melbourne)

lore: The Roman poet Juvenal called a perfect wife 'a rare bird in the lands, very like a black swan', and the phrase stood for the impossible until Willem de Vlamingh's crew saw black swans in 1697. It is the state emblem of Western Australia.
funFact: It appears on the flag and coat of arms of Western Australia, whose capital stands on the Swan River named after it.

summary: A fish-eating hawk found on every continent except Antarctica, diving feet-first to snatch fish from the water. Its recovery after the banning of DDT is one of conservation's great comeback stories.
nativeRange: Nearly worldwide: breeds across the Northern Hemisphere and Australasia; winters in the tropics and southern continents
abilities: Plunges feet-first into water, sometimes submerging fully
Reversible outer toe and spiny foot pads grip slippery fish
Carries fish head-forward to reduce drag
Long-distance migrant: some Scandinavian and Scottish birds winter in West Africa

animal.diet: Almost entirely live fish
animal.habitat: Coasts, lakes, rivers, reservoirs and estuaries
animal.behaviour: It hovers briefly over water, then folds its wings and dives, throwing its feet forward at the last moment.
fieldMarks: Dark brown upperparts, clean white underparts
White head with a bold dark stripe through the yellow eye
Long, narrow wings held in a gull-like crook with dark carpal patches
Brownish breast band, stronger in females
animal.voice: A series of high, clear, whistled 'cheep-cheep-cheep' or 'kyew' calls, often in flight near the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Large gulls share the crooked-wing shape but lack the hooked bill and dark eye-stripe. Juvenile bald eagles and white-tailed eagles are much larger and mottled below.
animal.whereToSee: Loch Garten and Rutland Water (UK), Chesapeake Bay and Florida (USA), Baltic coasts, Red Sea and Gulf of California; wintering in West Africa and South America
animal.season: Summer visitor to the Northern Hemisphere (Mar–Sep); winter visitor to the tropics; resident in Australia and some subtropical regions

lore: Ospreys were extinct as breeders in England by 1840 and in Scotland by 1916; their return to Loch Garten in 1954 and translocation to Rutland Water in the 1990s became milestones of British conservation.
funFact: Its family, Pandionidae, contains only the ospreys (one species, or two where the eastern osprey is split), and it is one of the most widely distributed birds in the world.

summary: A ghostly pale owl with a heart-shaped face that can hunt in total darkness by sound alone. It is one of the most studied predators in the world for its hearing.
nativeRange: Europe, Africa, the Middle East and western Asia
abilities: Can locate and catch prey in complete darkness using hearing alone
Asymmetrically placed ears pinpoint sounds in both direction and height
Soft, fringed feathers make its flight almost silent
Facial disc acts as a dish to focus sound

animal.diet: Small mammals, especially voles, mice and shrews
animal.habitat: Open grassland, farmland and marshes with old buildings or hollow trees
animal.lifespan: Usually under 4 years in the wild; record over 15 years
animal.behaviour: It quarters low over fields on silent wings, listening for rustling voles.
animal.voice: A long, rasping, eerie screech; also hisses and snores at the nest.
animal.lookalikes: Short-eared owl has yellow eyes, streaked plumage and a round face. Eastern and American barn owls (now separate species) are very similar but live in other regions.
animal.whereToSee: Farmland and marshes across Europe and Africa; East Anglia (UK), Camargue (France), South African grassland

lore: In European folklore the screeching barn owl was a bird of ill omen, called 'screech owl' or 'church owl'. Farmers in Israel and Jordan now put up nest boxes for barn owls as joint pest control across borders.
funFact: A barn owl pair may eat several thousand rodents in a single year.

summary: The second-largest penguin, standing nearly a metre tall, with brilliant orange ear patches. Its breeding cycle is so long that pairs can raise at most two chicks every three years.
nativeRange: Sub-Antarctic islands: South Georgia, Crozet, Kerguelen, Marion, Macquarie, Falklands; Tierra del Fuego
abilities: Dives to over 300 m deep in search of lanternfish
Incubates its egg on its feet beneath a fold of skin
Chicks are fed through winter by parents who may be away for weeks

animal.diet: Lanternfish and squid
animal.habitat: Open ocean; breeds on flat beaches and valleys on sub-Antarctic islands
animal.lifespan: Up to about 25 years in the wild
animal.behaviour: Brown, woolly chicks gather in creches through the winter while parents feed far at sea.
fieldMarks: Orange-yellow upper breast fading to white
Long, slender bill with orange-pink stripe
animal.voice: A loud, trumpeting call, used to find mates and chicks in colonies.
animal.lookalikes: Emperor penguin is larger and stockier, with paler yellow neck patches that are not enclosed by black, and breeds on Antarctic ice rather than sub-Antarctic beaches.
animal.whereToSee: Salisbury Plain, St Andrews Bay and Gold Harbour (South Georgia), Volunteer Point (Falklands), Crozet, Bahía Inútil (Chile)
animal.season: Present year-round at colonies; breeding cycle 14–16 months

lore: In the 19th and early 20th centuries king penguins were rendered for oil in great numbers on Macquarie Island and elsewhere.
funFact: Brown chicks were once thought to be a separate species, nicknamed 'woolly penguins'.

summary: The classic tuxedoed penguin of the Antarctic coast, breeding in vast colonies on ice-free ground. Each winter it follows the pack ice on migrations of thousands of kilometres.
nativeRange: Coasts of Antarctica
abilities: Undertakes winter migrations averaging about 13,000 km in the Ross Sea, following the sun and sea ice
Builds nests of pebbles that lift eggs above meltwater; stones are frequently stolen from neighbours
Dives to around 175 m, though most feeding dives are much shallower
Can toboggan on its belly across snow and ice

animal.diet: Krill, fish and squid
animal.habitat: Antarctic coasts and pack ice
animal.behaviour: Birds return to the same colony and often the same nest each October, walking up to tens of kilometres across sea ice to reach it.
fieldMarks: Bold white ring around the dark eye
Short bill largely covered by black feathers
Black back, white belly; short tail that often drags on the snow
animal.voice: A loud, rhythmic, throbbing bray given with the head pointed skyward in the 'ecstatic display'; growls and gargles when squabbling.
animal.lookalikes: Chinstrap penguin has a white face and throat crossed by a thin black chin strap. Gentoo penguin has an orange-red bill and a white stripe across the crown. Juvenile Adélies have a white throat but lack the chinstrap line and have a dark eye without the full white ring.
animal.whereToSee: Cape Royds and Cape Adare (Ross Sea), Paulet Island and Hope Bay (Antarctic Peninsula)
animal.season: Breeds at colonies October–February; winters at sea in the pack ice

lore: Jules Dumont d'Urville named it in 1840 after his wife Adèle. George Murray Levick's notes on its sexual behaviour from Scott's 1910–13 expedition were considered too shocking to publish and appeared only in 2012.
funFact: Subfossil remains show that Adélie penguins have used some Ross Sea colony sites for thousands of years, letting scientists track past climate through their bones and eggshell.

summary: A pirate of tropical seas with a huge red throat pouch in breeding males. It can stay aloft for days and steals fish from other seabirds.
nativeRange: Tropical Atlantic and eastern Pacific coasts
abilities: Lowest wing-loading of any bird, allowing effortless soaring
Steals fish from boobies and other seabirds
Can stay aloft for days at a time, even sleeping in flight
Males inflate a red throat pouch to attract females

animal.diet: Fish, squid, stolen prey
animal.habitat: Tropical coasts and islands
animal.behaviour: It chases other seabirds until they drop their catch, snatching it in mid-air.
fieldMarks: Males black with a red throat pouch
animal.voice: Silent at sea; drumming and rattling at colonies.
animal.lookalikes: Great frigatebird males have a green rather than purple gloss on the back and a pale wing bar; females have a red eye-ring and a pale grey throat. Lesser frigatebird is smaller, with white 'armpit' spurs. At distance the shape, long forked tail and angular wings separate frigatebirds from all other seabirds.
animal.whereToSee: Codrington Lagoon (Barbuda), North Seymour (Galápagos), Isla Contoy and Isla Isabel (Mexico), Florida Keys

lore: Sailors called it the man-o'-war bird for its piratical habits.
funFact: Its plumage is not fully waterproof, so it avoids landing on the sea and feeds by snatching prey from the surface or from other birds.

summary: A chocolate-brown seabird that makes one of the longest migrations of any animal, a figure-of-eight loop of the Pacific of some 64,000 km a year.
nativeRange: Breeds on islands around New Zealand, southern Chile and the Falklands; ranges throughout Pacific and Atlantic
abilities: Migrates up to 64,000 km a year
Dives to nearly 70 m
Shears low over waves on stiff wings
Uses burrows up to a metre or more deep, returning at night to avoid predators

animal.diet: Fish, squid and krill
animal.habitat: Open ocean; breeds in burrows on islands
animal.behaviour: Rafts of thousands gather off coasts during migration.
animal.voice: Silent at sea; moaning calls at burrows.
animal.lookalikes: Short-tailed shearwater is smaller with less silvery underwings. Flesh-footed shearwater has a pale bill and dark underwings.
animal.whereToSee: Monterey Bay (California), off Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, New Zealand coasts and the Tītī (Muttonbird) Islands off Stewart Island / Rakiura
animal.season: Breeds Nov–Apr (Southern Hemisphere); in North Pacific and Atlantic May–Sep

lore: Rakiura Māori harvest tītī chicks on the Tītī Islands under customary rights.
funFact: Satellite tracking published in 2006 showed birds from New Zealand flying a figure-of-eight loop to feeding grounds off Japan, Alaska or California and back, about 64,000 km in a year.

summary: The smallest booby and the only one that habitually nests in trees and shrubs, gripping branches with its bright red webbed feet. It plunge-dives for fish and squid far out in tropical oceans.
nativeRange: Tropical islands of the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic Oceans and the Caribbean
abilities: Plunge-dives from height into the sea after fish and squid
Catches flying fish in the air as they leap from the water
Forages hundreds of kilometres from the colony and often feeds at night or dusk
Occurs in several colour morphs, from white to all-brown

animal.diet: Flying fish and squid
animal.habitat: Pelagic tropical waters; nests in trees and bushes on remote islands
animal.behaviour: It often follows ships, catching flying fish flushed by the bow.
fieldMarks: Pale blue-grey bill with pink facial skin at the base
Variable plumage: all-white with black flight feathers, brown, or white-tailed brown morph
animal.voice: Mostly silent at sea; harsh, rattling squawks at the colony.
animal.lookalikes: Masked (and Nazca) booby is larger, with a black facial mask, yellow-orange or dull feet and black tail. Brown booby has a sharply demarcated dark brown head and breast and yellow feet. Only the red-footed booby has red feet.
animal.whereToSee: Genovesa Island (Galápagos), Kīlauea Point (Kauaʻi, Hawaiʻi), Little Cayman, Christmas Island, Aldabra
animal.season: Resident at colonies; breeding season varies by island

lore: The name 'booby' is usually traced to the Spanish 'bobo' (fool), from the birds' tameness when sailors landed on their islands.
funFact: The colony on Little Cayman, of several thousand pairs, is one of the largest in the Caribbean.

summary: A big, grey-brown coastal pelican that hunts by spectacular plunge-dives, unlike most other pelicans. It recovered from near disappearance in North America after DDT was banned.
nativeRange: Atlantic, Gulf and Pacific coasts of the Americas, from the USA to northern South America, and the Caribbean
abilities: Plunge-dives from up to about 20 m, folding back its wings before impact
Air sacs under the skin cushion the impact and help it bob back to the surface
Throat pouch holds up to about 10 litres of water and fish
Glides in lines just above wave crests, riding the air cushion

animal.diet: Small schooling fish such as menhaden, anchovies and sardines
animal.habitat: Coastal waters, bays, estuaries and mangrove islands
animal.behaviour: Laughing gulls often perch on a pelican's head to snatch fish spilling from its pouch.
fieldMarks: Grey-brown body; the smallest and darkest pelican
White head and neck in non-breeders; chestnut hindneck in breeding adults
Long bill with grey pouch (reddish in Pacific breeding birds)
Juveniles all brown with paler belly
animal.voice: Adults are almost silent; nestlings squeal and grunt.
animal.lookalikes: American white pelican is white with black flight feathers and feeds by swimming, not diving. Peruvian pelican (Peru and Chile) is larger, with a white stripe running down the neck.
animal.whereToSee: Florida Gulf Coast, Louisiana marshes, Monterey Bay and San Diego (California), Gulf of California, Caribbean islands
animal.season: Resident; Pacific birds disperse north after breeding

lore: San Francisco's Alcatraz Island takes its name from the Spanish 'alcatraces', for the pelicans that lived there. The brown pelican is the state bird of Louisiana and appears on its flag.
funFact: Removed from the US endangered species list in 2009, it is one of the clearest success stories of the DDT ban.

summary: A large, oily-black diving bird found on coasts and inland waters across much of the world. It pursues fish underwater using its feet and has been trained by fishermen in China for centuries.
nativeRange: Europe, Asia, Africa, Australasia and the North Atlantic coast of North America
abilities: Chases fish underwater, propelled by large webbed feet
Partly wettable plumage reduces buoyancy for diving
Dries wings by spreading them in a heraldic pose
Can dive to more than 30 m

animal.diet: Fish
animal.habitat: Coasts, estuaries, lakes and rivers
animal.lifespan: Usually around 11 years, recorded to over 20
animal.behaviour: Groups sometimes hunt together, driving fish into shallows.
fieldMarks: Black with bronze or blue sheen
White thigh patches in breeding season
Heavy hooked bill with bare yellow skin at base
Swims low in the water with head tilted up
animal.voice: Generally silent away from colonies; deep guttural croaks at nests.
animal.lookalikes: European shag is smaller and slimmer, with a thinner bill, greenish gloss and in spring a tufted crest; it lacks the white cheek patch. Double-crested cormorant (North America) has an orange throat pouch without white surround.
animal.whereToSee: Coastal and inland waters of Europe and Asia; Lake Naivasha (Kenya), the Li River at Guilin (China), Rutland Water (UK)

lore: In China, fishermen have trained great cormorants to fish for centuries, putting a snare around the bird's neck so that it cannot swallow large fish. Milton's Paradise Lost has Satan perch on the Tree of Life 'like a cormorant'.
funFact: The name cormorant comes from the Latin 'corvus marinus', sea-raven.

summary: A plump white scavenger of Antarctic penguin and seal colonies, and the only bird breeding in Antarctica that lacks webbed feet. It lives by stealing, cleaning up and scavenging.
nativeRange: Antarctic Peninsula, South Georgia, South Orkney and South Shetland Islands; winters south to Patagonia and the Falklands
abilities: Steals krill from penguins by startling them while they are feeding chicks
Eats eggs, carcasses, faeces and placentas of seals
Can fly long distances over the sea despite its pigeon-like appearance

animal.diet: Carrion, eggs, krill, seal placentas and faeces, and refuse
animal.habitat: Rocky coasts near penguin, cormorant and seal colonies; research stations
animal.behaviour: It patrols penguin colonies, harassing adults until they spill krill, which it snatches.
fieldMarks: Horny sheath over base of the yellowish bill
Short pinkish-grey legs and unwebbed feet
animal.voice: Harsh, crow-like 'caw' calls and scolding chatter.
animal.lookalikes: Black-faced sheathbill (southern Indian Ocean islands) has a black bill and face. Pigeons do not occur in Antarctica.
animal.whereToSee: Antarctic Peninsula landings (Port Lockroy, Brown Bluff), South Georgia, Falklands in winter
animal.season: Present in Antarctic summer; many winter in Falklands and Patagonia

lore: Early sealers and explorers called sheathbills 'paddies' and noted their fearlessness around camps.
funFact: Sheathbills are thought to be related to shorebirds such as plovers, despite their pigeon-like look.

summary: The most widespread and numerous albatross, with a dark 'eyebrow' giving it a stern expression. About two-thirds of the world population breeds in the Falkland Islands.
nativeRange: Breeds on sub-Antarctic islands (Falklands, South Georgia, Chile); ranges over the Southern Ocean
abilities: Dynamic soaring lets it travel thousands of kilometres with little flapping
Locks its wings in place with a shoulder tendon
Nests in vast colonies on cliffs and slopes

animal.diet: Fish, squid, crustaceans and fishery discards
animal.habitat: Open ocean; nests on sub-Antarctic islands
animal.behaviour: Pairs reunite every year with elaborate dances of bill-fencing and sky-pointing.
fieldMarks: Bright orange-yellow bill with reddish tip
Dark upperwings and back, white body
Broad dark margins to the white underwing
animal.voice: Braying and groaning calls at colonies; silent at sea.
animal.lookalikes: Campbell albatross (New Zealand) has a pale yellow eye. Shy albatross has a pale grey-green bill and narrow underwing margins.
animal.whereToSee: Steeple Jason, Saunders and New Islands (Falklands); off Cape Horn
animal.season: Breeds Sept–April; disperses north in winter

lore: The species was downlisted from Endangered to Near Threatened in 2013 and to Least Concern in 2017, following reductions in seabird bycatch.
funFact: Steeple Jason Island in the Falklands holds well over 100,000 breeding pairs, among the largest albatross colonies anywhere.

summary: The fastest-swimming penguin, with a white bonnet stripe and a bright orange bill. Its population has grown and spread south on the Antarctic Peninsula as sea ice declines.
nativeRange: Antarctic Peninsula and sub-Antarctic islands
abilities: Swims at up to about 36 km/h, the fastest of any penguin
Dives to around 200 m
Builds nests from stones and moss

animal.diet: Krill, fish and squid
animal.habitat: Coastal ice-free plains and beaches
animal.behaviour: Pairs build stone nests and may give pebbles as gifts.
fieldMarks: Broad white stripe over the head
animal.voice: Loud, trumpeting braying.
animal.lookalikes: Adélie has an all-black head and short bill. Chinstrap has a black chin strap.
animal.whereToSee: Port Lockroy (Antarctic Peninsula), Falklands, South Georgia

lore: The name 'gentoo' may come from an Anglo-Indian word for Hindu, but its origin is uncertain.
funFact: A 2020 genetic study proposed splitting the gentoo into four species across its range; most checklists still treat it as one.

summary: A sparrow-sized seabird that breeds in Antarctica and migrates to the North Atlantic. It is one of the most abundant birds on Earth and appears to 'walk' on water while feeding.
nativeRange: Breeds in Antarctica and sub-Antarctic islands; winters across all oceans
abilities: Pats the water with its feet while hovering, appearing to walk on it
Migrates from Antarctica to the North Atlantic each year
Finds food by smell

animal.diet: Krill, small fish, plankton
animal.habitat: Open ocean; breeds in rock crevices
animal.behaviour: It dances over the waves with feet pattering the water as it feeds.
fieldMarks: Long legs that project beyond the square tail
animal.voice: Silent at sea; chattering at nests.
animal.lookalikes: Leach's storm petrel has a forked tail. European storm petrel has a white underwing bar.
animal.whereToSee: Antarctic Peninsula; off North Carolina and Massachusetts in summer

lore: Sailors called storm petrels 'Mother Carey's chickens', thought to be from 'Mater Cara', the Virgin Mary.
funFact: The name 'petrel' is said to come from St Peter walking on water.
